section_summary.extract_value: This section introduces and qualifies the traditional threshold hypothesis, which suggests intelligence is necessary but not sufficient for creativity. The authors propose a 'conditional threshold hypothesis,' arguing that the intelligence-creativity relationship strengthens when other individual differences are also high, leading to differential relationships. They support this with theoretical arguments from Eysenck (1995) and Mackinnon (1962, 1965), and empirical evidence from Jauk et al. (2014) and King et al. (1996), highlighting the multiplicative effects of traits on creative achievement. The section also reinterprets Guilford's (1967) foundational work and Kim's (2005) meta-analysis to suggest that variability in the intelligence-creativity relationship at higher intelligence levels indicates the presence of ignored moderating variables.
